firstLayer.whatItDoes: LDL particles carry cholesterol from the liver through the circulation. LDL-C measures the cholesterol inside these particles, not their number; ApoB helps assess the number of atherogenic particles.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Higher LDL-C may reflect inherited lipid handling, saturated-fat intake, thyroid disease, certain medicines, or metabolic conditions. Low LDL-C can follow lipid-lowering treatment and is not automatically harmful.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Long-term exposure to LDL-containing particles contributes to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Absolute risk depends on age, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and other factors; a single result is not a diagnosis.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Review ApoB/non-HDL cholesterol and overall cardiovascular risk with the clinician when appropriate. Dietary substitution toward unsaturated fats and soluble fibre can support lipid management.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: Apolipoprotein B is a protein carried by potentially artery-depositing lipoprotein particles. Each LDL, VLDL remnant and Lp(a) particle generally carries one ApoB molecule, making ApoB an indicator of particle number.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Higher values often accompany insulin resistance, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, inherited lipid disorders or elevated LDL. Low values can occur with effective lipid-lowering treatment or rare lipid disorders.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: The number of ApoB-containing particles helps describe atherosclerotic risk, sometimes more clearly than LDL-C when cholesterol and particle number disagree.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Compare ApoB with LDL-C, non-HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and cardiovascular risk context. This protein measurement does not reveal an APOB gene mutation.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: Triglycerides are energy-storing fats transported in blood lipoproteins. The blood test measures circulating triglyceride concentration, which can vary with meals and fasting.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Higher concentrations can accompany alcohol use, excess energy intake, diabetes or insulin resistance, some medicines, inherited disorders, or a nonfasting sample. Very low results are not a general treatment target.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Elevated triglyceride-rich remnants can accompany increased cardiovascular risk; very high concentrations may warrant prompt evaluation because pancreatitis risk rises. One value does not identify a cause.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Check fasting status and trends alongside HDL, ApoB and glucose-related results; discuss marked elevations promptly. Physical activity and reduced alcohol and refined-carbohydrate excess may help, depending on context.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: HDL particles participate in transporting cholesterol and other lipids among tissues and the liver. HDL-C measures cholesterol carried within HDL particles, not how effectively HDL performs those functions.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Lower HDL-C commonly accompanies insulin resistance, elevated triglycerides, smoking, sedentary habits or certain medicines. Very high HDL-C is not necessarily protective and may have genetic or other causes.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Low HDL-C is associated with cardiovascular risk, but raising HDL-C alone has not reliably improved cardiovascular outcomes. The overall lipid profile and risk factors matter more than treating HDL-C in isolation.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Look at LDL-C, ApoB or non-HDL cholesterol and triglycerides together. Lifestyle choices should aim to improve cardiovascular health overall, not chase a higher HDL number alone.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: ALT is an enzyme concentrated in liver cells and involved in amino-acid metabolism. A blood ALT result reflects enzyme leakage into blood, not how well the liver performs all its functions.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Elevations can occur with liver fat accumulation, viral hepatitis, medicines or supplements, alcohol-related injury and occasionally intense exercise. A low result usually has much less specific meaning.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Persistent elevation can prompt evaluation of liver injury; normal ALT does not exclude steatosis or fibrosis. Results are interpreted with AST, GGT, other liver tests and clinical history.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Review trends, medications/supplements, recent exercise and any known liver imaging. Significant or persistent abnormalities warrant professional interpretation rather than choosing a supplement to lower ALT.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: AST participates in amino-acid metabolism and is present in liver and skeletal muscle, among other tissues. Blood AST therefore reflects more than liver biology.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Elevations can arise from liver injury, recent strenuous exercise, muscle injury, some medications and other conditions. A low value is rarely a stand-alone clinical problem.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: AST alongside ALT can provide context, but an AST/ALT ratio alone does not diagnose an underlying disease. When muscle contribution is possible, symptoms and sometimes creatine kinase may matter.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Compare AST with ALT, GGT, the original sample date and recent exercise or illness. A clinician can judge whether follow-up testing is needed.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: GGT is an enzyme involved in glutathione-related amino-acid transfer and is found especially in liver and biliary tissues. Blood GGT is often interpreted with other liver enzymes.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Higher results can accompany bile-duct or liver conditions, alcohol exposure, metabolic disorders and some medications. Low GGT generally does not carry the same significance as elevation.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: GGT is sensitive but not specific: it cannot by itself identify the cause of liver injury. With raised alkaline phosphatase it may help distinguish a liver/biliary origin from bone-related findings.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Review the pattern with ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, medications, alcohol and any symptoms; persistent abnormalities deserve clinician review.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: Glucose fuels cells, particularly the brain, and is regulated by insulin, liver glucose production and tissue uptake. A blood result captures glucose at the time the sample was taken.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: A high value may follow food intake, physiological stress, certain medicines or impaired glucose regulation. Low values can occur with fasting, medications, endocrine conditions or other situations; symptoms and sample context matter.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Fasting, random and challenge-test results use different interpretation rules. One result does not establish diabetes or explain persistent symptoms.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Check whether the sample was fasting, compare with HbA1c when appropriate, and discuss repeatedly abnormal values or symptomatic lows with a clinician.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: HbA1c is the fraction of haemoglobin that has glucose attached to it. It approximates exposure to glucose over the preceding two to three months, not a single-day glucose reading.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Higher results often reflect sustained higher blood glucose. An unexpectedly low or discordant result can arise with altered red-cell lifespan, blood loss, haemolysis or assay-related factors.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: HbA1c is useful in diabetes screening and monitoring when appropriate criteria are met, but anaemia, haemoglobin variants and some medical conditions can make it misleading.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Compare with measured glucose and the lab method; if the two disagree, consider discussing red-cell factors or alternative monitoring with the clinician.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: Vitamin B12 supports DNA synthesis, red-blood-cell production and nervous-system function. Serum B12 measures circulating vitamin, which is an imperfect proxy for cellular availability.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Lower results can reflect limited intake, absorption problems, pernicious anaemia or medications such as metformin and long-term acid suppression. High values may follow supplementation or accompany other conditions.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: A borderline B12 result alone cannot confirm or rule out functional deficiency; methylmalonic acid can sometimes clarify status, though kidney function influences it.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Review diet, supplements, medicines, blood count and symptoms. Discuss further testing with a clinician if results are borderline or symptoms suggest deficiency; do not infer need from genetics alone.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the main circulating storage marker used to assess vitamin D status. It is not the same test as active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and does not directly measure vitamin D intake.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Lower values can reflect limited sun exposure, intake, absorption or certain health conditions; higher levels often reflect supplementation and occasionally excessive intake.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Vitamin D supports calcium absorption and bone metabolism. Thresholds and testing indications vary by guidance and clinical circumstances; a number alone cannot establish a cause or safe dose.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Review the precise assay, supplement amounts and bone-health context. Avoid escalating vitamin D supplementation solely to optimize a number without reviewing intake and safety.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: Ferritin is the principal cellular iron-storage protein. Blood ferritin often reflects iron stores but is also affected by inflammation and liver or other illness.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Low ferritin commonly suggests reduced iron stores, for example with blood loss or inadequate intake. High ferritin can reflect inflammation, liver disease, iron loading or several other causes.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Ferritin is not interchangeable with serum iron or transferrin saturation; high ferritin alone does not diagnose iron overload. Low ferritin can be clinically meaningful before overt anaemia.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Compare with CBC, transferrin saturation, symptoms, inflammation and any blood-loss history; seek clinician advice rather than taking iron automatically.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism, DNA synthesis and red-blood-cell formation. Serum folate captures circulating folate and can respond to recent dietary or supplement intake.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Low results may accompany limited intake, malabsorption or increased needs. High values often reflect fortified foods or supplements and are not automatically evidence of better function.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Low folate may contribute to megaloblastic anaemia and elevated homocysteine, but B12-related disease must be considered separately before high-dose folic acid use.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: Review food patterns, supplements, B12 and blood count with a clinician if low or discordant. Serum folate and red-cell folate are distinct tests.

firstLayer.whatItDoes: Homocysteine is formed during methionine metabolism. Folate, vitamin B12 and vitamin B6 participate in its recycling or breakdown; the test measures its blood concentration.
firstLayer.whyLowHigh: Higher results may reflect inadequate B-vitamin status, reduced kidney function, hypothyroidism, medicines, smoking or other factors. An MTHFR variant alone does not establish the cause.
firstLayer.whyItMatters: Higher homocysteine is associated with vascular outcomes, but vitamin treatment to lower the number has not consistently reduced heart attacks or strokes in most people. Low results usually need less attention.
firstLayer.whatToDiscuss: If elevated, consider discussing B12, folate, kidney function, thyroid context and medicines with a clinician rather than assuming a genetic or dietary diagnosis.
